¶ 366

Two verses apart

09:47

Rabbi Yitzchak opens with a problem in the plain text. Genesis 48 says Israel saw Joseph's sons. Two verses later it says his eyes were heavy with age and he could not see. If he could not see, what does "and Israel saw" mean?

Genesis 48:8

And Israel saw Joseph's sons and said, "Who are these?"

Genesis 48:10

And Israel's eyes were heavy with age; he could not see.

An old, sick man near the end of his life. He recognizes the son he loves, squints at two figures beside him, and asks who they are. Nothing more.
¶ 366

What he saw from afar

11:35

Jacob saw b'ruach kudsha, with divine inspiration. Not two grandsons but their descendants, and one descendant in particular. Tap through the line from Jacob to the two golden calves.

Ephraim and Menashe stand in front of their grandfather. Jacob asks who they are.
¶ 366

The same word, twice

14:13

The Zohar's proof is one word. Yoravam's declaration over his calves copies the golden calf in the desert, and Jacob's question uses the same word that both declarations hang on: ele, "these."

Exodus 32:4
The golden calf

Ele elohecha Yisrael — These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.

1 Kings 12:28
Yoravam's two calves

Hine elohecha Yisrael — Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.

Genesis 48:8
Jacob

Mi ele? — Who are these?

So the question reads: who are these, the ones who will one day say "these are your gods"? Physically blind, Jacob saw the two calves and trembled.

¶ 367–368

Tzadikim see the end

16:23

From here: the righteous see from a distance, as the Creator sees. On the sixth day "God saw all that He had made, and it was very good" means He saw the whole future of creation before it was created. Every generation, from one end of the world to the other, stands before Him before it arrives.

The class told a Hanukkah-season story to show what "seeing the end" means in practice. Step through it.

An innkeeper, a student, and a teacher

Yaakov Yitzchak of Lublin · student

Rabbi Elimelech of Lizhensk · teacher

At the end it is always good. If it is not good, it is not yet the end.

This is also why the Creator loves every person. He does not judge the current circumstance. He sees the inevitable goodness that will be revealed from that soul.

¶ 369

The Book of Adam

29:23

The righteous also see every generation before it comes. The source is Adam, who was shown all of humanity before any of it existed. The verse is from this week's portion: Zeh sefer toldot Adam, "this is the book of the generations of Adam" (Genesis 5:1).

The Zohar reads it as an actual book: twelve sequences of three letters, in which the Creator showed Adam the perfected path of every soul. Your name is in it. Scanning the letters connects you to the version of your life the Creator intended, which is a purpose larger than your own ability. It only becomes possible with divine assistance, and the assistance comes when you want that life.

01

Know the path exists

Your perfected life was prepared before creation and shown to Adam and to Moses. Certainty first.

02

Want it more than your comfort

Be willing to do the work written there, however uncomfortable. No one lives their purpose by accident.

03

Receive the help

When the desire is real, the Creator gives the wisdom, strength and direction to live up to your name.

¶ 370

Two questions, one answer

33:30

"Who are these?" was two questions at once: who are these two boys, and who are those descendants who will say "these are your gods." Joseph answered only the first: "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." Right now they are holy, both of them, both from the light.

How do we know Jacob was shown the future? From the word gam: "God has shown me also your seed." Not only the children in front of him. Also everything that would come from them.
